findings.text: Boot-time self check builds a range-populated tree with an externally locked configuration, duplicates it into a second tree, rewrites every entry in the copy through a full-range walk, then validates and tears down both trees.
Boot-time benchmark populates one locked tree once and then repeatedly initialises, duplicates, rewrites, validates and destroys a fresh destination tree for a large fixed iteration count.

Self check populates fixed-size adjacent ranges and then exercises bounded forward walks, mid-walk overwrite of a cursor window, and successor lookup after the bound to confirm the cursor advances correctly.

Self check covers forward and backward cursor motion across gaps, across node boundaries and across two tree levels, plus running off either end and stepping back, including behaviour after removal of the first entry.
Self check copies all entries from one tree to another by walking the source under cursor and read-side protection while storing each observed window into the destination, then validates the copy.
Self check builds many small ranges then performs a wide clearing store spanning many entries.

Regression collection replays numbered insert, store, erase, load and range-store sequences, each starting from a fresh tree and ending with teardown, targeting spanning rebalance, overflow and metadata defects described in its own notes.
Duplication preserves the full ordered entry set: the destination walk observes every source value and can rewrite each in place without changing membership before successful validation.
Forward iteration over adjacent fixed-size ranges visits values in strictly increasing key order with the cursor window exactly matching each stored range.
After a bounded iteration, a successor query returns the entry following the previous bound, including the split remainder created by an overlapping mid-iteration overwrite.
Lookup of an unpopulated gap yields absence while neighbouring populated windows retain their distinct values, and stepping forward then backward returns to the prior entry.

Stepping past the last entry reports absence with a trailing gap extending to the maximum key, and stepping before the first entry reports absence at the start; both positions can step back onto the adjacent real entry, with an underflow indicator for the start case.

Trees configured for external locking depend on caller-owned read-write semaphores held in write mode across population, duplication and teardown, with the second tree acquired under a nested subclass to express a fixed lock order.
Cursor access is bracketed by explicit lock and unlock operations around walks and stores, and some traversals additionally hold a read-side critical section across the locked walk.

Cursor progresses through selection, positioned walk, bounded iteration or stepwise next and previous moves, optional pause and reset, and terminal destroy; stores may be issued from a positioned cursor and affect later successor results.
Out-of-memory duplication failure is treated as fatal: the failure is logged and execution halts rather than continuing with a partial copy.
Validation is invoked on duplicated or copied trees before destruction, and internal consistency assertions abort the boot-time check on any mismatch of position, range or value.
A flag combination selects range-allocation behaviour with external locking, and a separate allocation-range-only mode exists for plain trees.
Kernel allocation mode is requested for range stores and duplication, the maximum unsigned key denotes an unbounded walk limit, and a single-depth nesting subclass orders the second write lock.
A compile-time width selector chooses between two sets of expected multi-level indices and entry counts, and a large sentinel toggles a non-kernel allocation test mode around some walks.

The observable cursor carries a current window with start and end keys plus a node handle and owning-tree link; tests assign the window directly before storing and compare node identity to detect crossing a node boundary.
